questions.q: Which amine gives brisk effervescence of N₂ from a clear solution when treated with NaNO₂ and dilute HCl at 273–278 K?
questions.explain: A 1° aliphatic amine forms a very unstable alkyldiazonium ion that loses N₂ at once. Aniline forms a diazonium salt that is stable in the cold, so no gas is seen.

questions.q: Diethylamine is treated with cold nitrous acid. The yellow oily product that separates is:
questions.explain: A 2° amine has only one N–H, so the reaction stops at the N-nitroso compound R₂N–N=O. Writing it as an N-nitro compound (R₂N–NO₂) is the common mistake.

questions.q: N,N-Dimethylaniline reacts with nitrous acid in the cold to give a green solid. What is it?
questions.explain: With no N–H, the strongly activating –NMe₂ group lets the weak electrophile NO⁺ attack the free para position of the ring. If the para position is blocked, no green nitroso compound forms.

questions.q: While testing an unknown amine, a student lets the NaNO₂/HCl mixture warm up and sees steady N₂ evolution. Why might this wrongly suggest a primary aliphatic amine?
options: A secondary amine loses N₂ from its nitrosamine on warming
A tertiary aliphatic amine is oxidised to N₂ when warm
A primary aromatic amine's diazonium salt decomposes to phenol and N₂ on warming
Nitrous acid alone decomposes to N₂ in the absence of an amine
questions.explain: Arenediazonium salts survive only in the cold; on warming they decompose to phenol with N₂ evolution. The mixture must be kept at 0–5 °C so that only 1° aliphatic amines give gas.
